title: An ordinary evening
hookLine: Seneca waits for the lamp to go out, then puts his own day on trial
tomorrow: what did the Prophet give his daughter instead of what she asked?

lines: SENECA WAITS FOR THE LAMP TO GO.
cards: Lights off, phone face down, and the replay starts: the thing you said in the meeting, the text you sent too fast. A Roman named Seneca had a stranger habit, and he tells us exactly when he did it.

Every night, once the lamp had been carried out of the room, and once his wife, who knew his habit, had gone quiet, he started on purpose. So why wait for the dark and the silence? What was he doing in there?

teach.h: SENECA PUTS HIS DAY ON TRIAL.
teach.b: He was putting his day on trial. Seneca was a Stoic philosopher, and he describes this in his book On Anger.
He took the habit from an older teacher, Sextius, who asked himself at the end of each day: what bad habit have you cured today? What fault have you resisted?
In what are you better? So Seneca pleads his own case every evening.
He goes over the whole day, his words and his deeds, and hides nothing from himself.

teach.h: A JUDGE, NOT JUST A PROSECUTOR.
teach.b: Then the surprise: the judge is kind. He even gives a sample verdict. In that argument you spoke too sharply; next time, don't take on people who won't learn.
See that you don't do it again; this time I forgive you.
That's the Stoic evening review as Seneca kept it: an honest look, one correction, a pardon, then sleep. Seneca says the sleep that follows is calm and deep. Now set that beside the midnight replay.

The replay is a court with only a prosecutor, and the case never closes. Seneca's court has a judge, and it ends with a sentence that lets you go to bed. Perhaps that's why he waited for the dark: the day was done.
The evening's job was to hear it once, fairly, and close the case.

how: Stoic readers keep Seneca's evening review: at day's end they go over what they said and did, name one thing to do better, and let the day close with a pardon rather than a replay.

o: the time to plan everything for the next morning
the tired hours that are left before you sleep
the hour the day gets one fair look, then closes

s: the Stoic evening review means beating yourself up over mistakes
the popular picture. Seneca hides nothing, but his verdict ends: this time I forgive you.
Seneca says he took the habit from an older teacher, Sextius
Sextius asked himself each night what bad habit he had cured that day.
Seneca did his review first thing in the morning
he did it at night, once the lamp was out and the house had gone quiet.

games.q: your roommate lies awake replaying a clumsy thing she said at work, over and over. what fits Seneca's evening rule?
o: go over it once, fairly: name the fix for next time, then pardon it.
keep replaying it until the feeling fades; that's how you learn.
don't look back at the day at all; it only makes things worse.
games.why: Seneca looked at the whole day and hid nothing, then forgave himself: see that you don't do it again. then he slept.

practice: Close your eyes and walk back through today, words and deeds, the way Seneca did. Stop at one moment you'd do differently, and give it a fair verdict in one sentence: next time, I'll do this instead.
Then pardon it, and let the rest of the sit be quiet.

wordCard.voice: An ordinary evening: for Seneca, not leftover time, but the hour when the day gets one honest hearing and then closes.

carryVoice: Your line: the evening is the day's fair hearing. Seneca's verdict ended in a pardon. Sleep well.

sources.ref: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira) 3.36: Sextius's three questions; the lamp removed, the wife silent; 'see that you do not do this again, this time I forgive you'; the sleep that follows
